scope: New provider word events and beat intervals for coordinate construction, forward arrival, chain replay, rounded ratio, optimizer separation, and unseen-request reveal regressions. No build, audio, or render paths required.

beats.say: Back at weight three, predict what an upward nudge will do. We already predict too much time. Increasing the weight should therefore raise the loss. Now move it to three point zero zero one.
The original loss is one. The new loss is a little above one, so the nudge moved uphill. The exact values are shown below the points; magnification lets us inspect that tiny change.
Divide the loss increase by the weight increase. The ratio is just above four. That positive slope tells us how rapidly loss rises when we turn the dial up.

Now split the prediction into prompt work and queue delay, with weights two and two. Turn only the prompt dial. A nudge of one hundredth raises loss by about four hundredths. Its local sensitivity is four.
Reset the prompt dial and turn only the queue dial. The same nudge raises loss by about two hundredths. Its sensitivity is two. These are partial derivatives: each question freezes the other weight.

Collect the slopes in parameter order. Four along the prompt coordinate, two along the queue coordinate. Their combined arrow is the gradient, four comma two. These components record sensitivity. The learning rate will scale their update.
Instead of nudging each weight, break our predictor into small operations. Record each operation's inputs for the backward pass.
The prompt branch produces four, and the queue branch produces two. Add them to get six. Subtract the fixed target, five, to get error one. Square it to get loss one.
That is the forward pass. Keep its error and feature values. Those same numbers will supply each weight's sensitivity on the backward pass.
Start with sensitivity one at the loss. The square has local slope twice the error, so one becomes two. Subtracting a fixed target has slope one, so two passes through unchanged.
Addition passes that two to both branches. The prompt weight acts through feature two, giving two times two equals four. The queue weight acts through feature one, giving two times one equals two.

Trace the prompt route. Start with one. The square contributes times two, subtraction times one, and the prompt feature another times two. Multiply the factors to recover four. Backpropagation organizes this chain rule across the graph.
On a small model, evaluate loss just above and below weight three. Divide the difference by twice the nudge, and compare with our reference derivative, four.
Agreement within a chosen tolerance supports the backward rule at this smooth point. Try other inputs too. At a sharp corner such as ReLU at zero, an ordinary derivative may not exist.

These near-equal losses were rounded before subtraction. In float thirty-two, dividing their difference by twice the nudge gives a slope estimate of about three point eight one five. Double precision stays close to four here; rounding error dominates the lower-precision ratio.
In PyTorch, ask the weights to require gradients. Clear the old gradient buffer, run the forward prediction, and compute a scalar loss. The stored weights themselves have not moved.
Backward fills the buffer with four comma two. The weights are still two comma two. Only the optimizer step applies learning rate one tenth, changing them to one point six and one point eight.

Send the same incoming gradient into two buffer histories. A cleared buffer finishes at four comma two. Keep the previous buffer and it finishes at eight comma four. Backward adds; clearing chooses the history.

Your turn. A new request has three prompt blocks and one second queued. It took seven seconds; our weights are two and two. Predict the model output, then the two gradient entries. Pause here if you want to calculate.

The prediction is eight, so error is one. Twice that error times each feature gives gradient six comma two. With learning rate zero point zero five, the new weights are one point seven and one point nine. Now the prediction is seven.
Try an unseen request: one prompt block, two seconds queued, observed time four. The model predicts five point five. Fitting one row gave us a useful update; generalization needs a new measurement.
